nameStory: Canadian milkvetch gets its name from its northern range extending throughout Canada, though it's found across much of North America. The "milkvetch" part comes from an old belief that these plants could increase milk production in grazing animals - "vetch" refers to climbing or sprawling legume plants that were traditionally used as livestock feed.
description: Canadian milkvetch is a sturdy perennial wildflower that grows 1-4 feet tall with a bushy, upright habit. Like other members of the legume family, it produces clusters of small pea-like flowers and compound leaves made up of many small leaflets. The cream-colored to pale yellow flowers bloom in dense, elongated clusters that stand above the foliage, creating an attractive display in summer meadows and woodland edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, cylindrical clusters of cream to pale yellow pea-like flowers, each about 1/2 inch long. The flower spikes feel firm and slightly fuzzy to the touch, standing upright like candles above the leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 15-25 oval leaflets arranged along a central stem. The leaflets feel smooth and slightly thick, and the whole leaf has a fresh, green bean-like smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in sturdy clumps 1-4 feet tall with multiple stems arising from the base. The plant has a robust, bushy appearance and feels substantial when you brush against it.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops inflated, papery pods that rattle when shaken and contain several hard, kidney-shaped seeds. The pods turn brown and feel crispy when mature.

habitat: In New England, Canadian milkvetch is quite rare, found in wetland edges, moist meadows, and prairie-like openings. It prefers rich, moist soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade, often growing alongside other moisture-loving wildflowers like joe-pye weed and New England asters.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the compound leaves unfurl, creating bushy mounds of fresh green foliage. Young plants are easiest to identify by their distinctive compound leaves with many small leaflets.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, when the cream-colored flower clusters are most prominent and fragrant. This is the best time for identification as the distinctive pea-like flowers are clearly visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the inflated seed pods develop, turning from green to brown and becoming papery. The foliage may begin to yellow but often stays green well into autumn.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only dried stems and scattered seed pods. The plant overwinters as underground roots and will regrow from the base in spring.

funFact: Canadian milkvetch is like a natural fertilizer factory - its roots form partnerships with special bacteria that capture nitrogen from the air and convert it into plant food, actually improving the soil for neighboring plants!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other legume wildflowers like wild senna or partridge pea, but Canadian milkvetch's dense, upright flower clusters and cream-colored blooms set it apart from the more scattered yellow flowers of these relatives. Remember: cream clusters = Canadian milkvetch.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's only found in Canada, this plant actually grows throughout much of North America. However, it's become quite rare in New England, with only a handful of known locations, making any sighting special and worth reporting to local botanists.
compareHints: Canadian milkvetch is much more robust and tall than its rare New England relatives like Robbins' milkvetch, which is a tiny alpine plant, or Alpine milkvetch, which stays close to the ground. The cream-colored flowers and large size make Canadian milkvetch the giant of the New England milkvetch family, though all share the characteristic compound leaves and pea-like flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Alpine Milkvetch which grows in high mountain areas, Robbins' Milkvetch is found at low elevations along rivers.
Alpine Milkvetch differs from its cousin Canadian Milkvetch by being much shorter and growing only in alpine zones, while Canadian Milkvetch grows tall in lowland prairies and fields.
Among New England's milkvetches, chickpea milkvetch is the most robust and bushy, staying under 3 feet tall.
